title: Foraging energetics reveals late‐summer challenges for pollinators across two British cities
content:
Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog.


Abstract

Foraging bees often work within fine energetic margins, but recent work has shown that foraging conditions can vary markedly across the year. Despite the importance of seasonality for pollinator foraging, most work in this area has relied on indirect approaches. However, energetic efficiency, the ratio of energetic gain to cost during foraging, can be quantified directly to provide a direct comparison of the seasonal foraging conditions experienced by nectar foragers. Here, we provide the first direct measure of seasonal changes in foraging conditions by tracking the energetic efficiency of honeybee nectar forgers across a whole season (April – October) on flower patches that colonies were naturally exploiting. We combined foraging observations, flower nectar sampling and physiological data from the literature to estimate foraging efficiency (ratio of energy net gain to energy expenditure) on 19 study plant species in two locations ~600 km apart in Britain, Brighton and Edinburgh. We found that foraging efficiency was lowest in late summer (mid-July – August), with predicted foraging efficiency reaching its lowest in mid-August. As honeybees are generalist foragers and continually monitor foraging conditions, our data suggest that foraging conditions may be challenging during late summer for other flower visitors. Similar patterns of energetic efficiency and energy per flower were observed for both study sites. However, the more urban site was less variable, highlighting the potential importance of land-use context for influencing seasonal continuity of floral resources. Our results provide the first direct assessment of seasonal variation in foraging efficiency of individual nectar foragers. Our results are relevant to conservation efforts and suggest that efforts to improve nectar general availability in Britain may be most valuable if provided in late summer.
